method: Independent second-pass review: load-bearing claims read against the cited source.

findings.claim: Standard sea-level pressure is 1013.25 hPa, equal to a column of about 10.3 tonnes of air per square metre

Dry air is 78.084% nitrogen, 20.946% oxygen, 0.934% argon; the top four constituents are 99.998% of the total; water vapour ranges from near zero over dry desert regions to approaching 4% in the tropics
NOAA's table lists carbon dioxide at 0.042 per cent, and the Global Monitoring Laboratory global annual mean is 425.62 +/- 0.09 ppm for 2025
NASA Glenn's standard atmosphere sets 15.04 C at the surface with a 0.00649 C/m decrease; pressure halves at about 5.5 km and is roughly 22% at 11 km; the lower stratosphere is near -56.5 C

Top-of-atmosphere solar intensity is about 1,360 W/m2 on the face presented to the Sun and about 340 W/m2 spread over the sphere; 29% is reflected, 23% absorbed in the atmosphere, 48% at the surface, so 71% (close to 240 W/m2) is absorbed
AR6 reports an Earth energy imbalance of 0.50 [0.32 to 0.69] W/m2 for 1971-2006 rising to 0.79 [0.52 to 1.06] W/m2 for 2006-2018, with ocean heat uptake accounting for 91% of the total energy change
NASA CERES puts the energy imbalance at approximately 0.7 W/m2, which it notes is 0.3 per cent of absorbed solar radiation
findings.note: The 0.7 W/m2 / 0.3% figures are on the page exactly as quoted, but the article called this the 'present magnitude'. The CERES science overview attaches no date or period to the number, and CERES EEI is a continuously updating record; the same chapter of AR6 already cited in this article assesses 0.79 W/m2 for 2006-2018, and NASA Earth Observatory says 'a little over 0.8'. Live dataset with no temporal anchor available in the source: removed the 'present' framing and said instead that the source states the figure without attaching a period, rather than inventing a date.

findings.claim: Opening summary: about five petawatts of energy is moved from the tropics towards each pole
findings.note: The 5 PW figure is the ANNUAL MEAN peak in Trenberth and Caron (2001); the same paper reports maxima exceeding 8 PW in Northern Hemisphere winter and much smaller summer values. The article said the transport happens 'continuously', which reads as a steady value. Replaced with 'in the annual mean', which is what the source supports.

findings.claim: Journal of Climate analysis finds atmospheric transport peaking at 5.0 +/- 0.14 PW at 43N with similar values near 40S; at 35 degrees the atmosphere carries 78% of the total in the Northern Hemisphere and 92% in the Southern; ocean transport dominates only between the equator and about 17N

AR6 puts CERES-EBAF surface downward solar and thermal flux uncertainties at 10 and 8 W/m2 and ocean latent and sensible heat flux uncertainties at roughly 11 and 5 W/m2; CMIP5 land-averaged downward thermal and solar radiation differ by more than 30 and 40 W/m2, with CMIP6 agreeing better; polar surface fluxes are least constrained because there are fewer surface sites

openQuestions: The CERES science overview gives no observation period for its 0.7 W/m2 imbalance figure, so the article can only say that the source states it undated. A dated CERES-EBAF release figure would be a better citation if the desk wants a specific period.

findings.claim: The Stefan-Boltzmann constant is 5.670374419 x 10^-8 W m-2 K-4 and CODATA now fixes it exactly
The Wien wavelength constant 2.897771955 x 10^-3 m K puts a 288 K peak at 10.06 um; the frequency constant 5.878925757 x 10^10 Hz K-1 gives a peak corresponding to 17.71 um for the same body
The Sun's surface is close to 5,800 K, putting its emission peak near 0.50 um; Earth's 255 K effective temperature (the value satisfying Stefan's law for roughly 240 W/m2) puts its peak near 11 um
The atmospheric window runs from roughly 8 to 14 um with maximum transparency near 10 um, and a strong carbon dioxide band sits between about 12 and 15 um
AR6 records that Angstrom's 1900 saturation assertion 'was understood half a century later to be incorrect'

Line-by-line calculations in JGR: Atmospheres found the logarithmic dependence holds even for monochromatic radiance, beyond what band-saturation arguments explain, and attributed it to an emission-layer displacement effect in an atmosphere with temperature falling linearly and gas concentration decaying exponentially with height
findings.sourceChecked: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/2014JD022466 (publisher-deposited abstract of Huang and Bani Shahabadi 2014; Wiley full text returned 403)

findings.claim: A 2016 GRL revision reports 1750-2011 CO2 forcing within 1 per cent of the previous assessed value but about 10 per cent higher at 2,000 ppm, and methane's forcing about 25 per cent higher, from 0.48 to 0.61 W/m2, once shortwave absorption is included
findings.sourceChecked: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1002/2016GL071930 (publisher-deposited abstract of Etminan et al. 2016; Wiley full text returned 403)

findings.claim: AR6's assessed effective radiative forcing for a doubling of carbon dioxide relative to 1750 is 3.93 +/- 0.47 W/m2
The NIST Chemistry WebBook entry cited as the reference spectrum is the gas-phase infrared spectrum of carbon dioxide

openQuestions: Both AGU papers are paywalled at Wiley (403 to scripted clients). Their claims were checked against the publisher-deposited abstracts via Crossref, which carry the exact figures quoted; the full texts were not read.

The molecular-symmetry argument (homonuclear diatomics have no dipole-active vibration; CO2's bending mode does) is standard textbook spectroscopy and was treated as background rather than checked against a source.

findings.claim: 240 W/m2 absorbed gives a 255 K effective emitting temperature against an observed surface near 288 K, which NASA Earth Observatory records as roughly 15 C and 'more than 30 degrees warmer than it would be if it didn't have an atmosphere'
The 33 K calculation holds planetary albedo fixed at its present value of about 0.29
NASA GISS attributed infrared absorption as roughly 50 per cent to water vapour, 25 per cent to clouds and 20 per cent to carbon dioxide, with the remainder from ozone, methane and aerosol
In flux terms the surface emits about 150 W/m2 more than what leaves for space
Taking a standard tropospheric decrease of about 6.5 K per kilometre, the 255 K level is roughly five kilometres above a 288 K surface
The Goddard analysis gives about 4 W/m2 of extra absorption from doubling carbon dioxide directly, rising to almost 20 W/m2 once water vapour and clouds have adjusted
Work published in Nature in 2001 inferred increases in greenhouse forcing from the outgoing longwave radiation spectra of the Earth in 1970 and 1997

Spectroscopic observations at the Southern Great Plains and North Slope of Alaska gave clear-sky CO2 surface forcing attributable to the 22 ppm rise from 2000 to 2010, with trends of 0.2 W/m2 per decade (+/- 0.06 and +/- 0.07), seasonal ranges of 0.1-0.2 W/m2, and roughly ten per cent of the trend in downwelling longwave radiation
NASA CERES puts the imbalance at approximately 0.7 W/m2, or 0.3 per cent of absorbed solar radiation, alongside the IPCC's 0.79 [0.52 to 1.06] W/m2 for 2006-2018
findings.note: Same live-dataset problem as in the pillar article: the numbers are on the CERES page verbatim, but the article called this 'the current imbalance' and the source attaches no period to it. Replaced 'current' with a statement that the science overview gives the figure without a period; the AR6 value beside it already carries its own 2006-2018 anchor and was left alone.

openQuestions: Harries et al. (2001) is paywalled; only the Nature abstract was read. The abstract supports the sentence as written (spectral differences attributed to CH4, CO2, O3, CFC-11 and CFC-12, described as direct experimental evidence of an increased greenhouse effect), but the band-specific detail was not checked against the full paper.

The GISS brief attaches its own hedge to the 4 -> 20 W/m2 result ('in the GISS climate model, at least'). The article attributes it to 'the Goddard analysis' and immediately says the multiplier is not well constrained, which was judged adequate; a desk that wants the model dependence stated outright would need one more clause.

findings.claim: The dry adiabatic lapse rate is a fixed 9.8 C per 1,000 metres
The moist adiabatic rate is about 4 C per 1,000 metres near the surface and rises towards the dry value in the upper troposphere
The standard atmosphere sets the environmental lapse rate at 0.00649 C per metre from a 15.04 C surface up to 11,000 metres
NOAA uses a ball-and-bowl analogy for the stability regimes and describes conditional instability as one of the most common states of the atmosphere

The Storm Prediction Center defines CAPE as the total potential energy available to a surface parcel lifted to its level of free convection, in joules per kilogram; 2,000 J/kg corresponds to an undiluted-parcel updraft of about 63 m/s

A Salt Lake valley field campaign ran from 1 December 2010 to 7 February 2011 and documented ten persistent cold-air pool episodes; 24-hour mean PM2.5 often exceeds the 35 ug/m3 NAAQS during such episodes, and did so during each of the four longest pools
The mechanism behind the pollution build-up is loss of dilution volume rather than extra emission
findings.note: The paper attributes the concentrations to CAP strength and duration but explicitly adds that 'variations in emissions may also play a role', naming reduced Christmas-holiday commuter traffic during IOP 4. The article's flat 'not extra emission' excluded something the source declines to exclude. Narrowed to 'the dominant mechanism' and added the authors' own caveat.

findings.claim: Stratospheric temperature climbs from about -51 C at the tropopause to roughly -15 C at the top; warmer air above cooler suppresses convection and flattens thunderstorm anvils; the stratosphere holds about 19 per cent of the atmosphere's mass; the troposphere reaches 18-20 km at the equator and about 6 km at the poles

The WMO lapse-rate tropopause definition as quoted, the second-tropopause 3 C/km criterion, mean tropical tropopause at 16-17 km and high-latitude at roughly 8-12.5 km, and ERA5-minus-ERA-Interim monthly mean height differences from about -300 m near 30 degrees to 150 m at the equator

openQuestions: The stability criteria stated in lapse-rate terms (environmental rate shallower than both adiabats = absolutely stable, etc.) are not on the cited NOAA pages, which give the buoyancy argument and the bowl analogy but not the numeric comparison. They are standard textbook definitions and consistent with what NOAA does say, so they were left as written rather than resourced.

The article says the stratosphere holds 19 per cent of the atmosphere's 'mass'; NOAA's wording is '19 percent of the atmosphere's gases'. Read as equivalent, but it is NOAA's phrase that was paraphrased, not a mass figure NOAA states.
